\chapter{Five Parts of a Building}
\label{ch:la-terraza-y-la-sala}
\hlchaptermodality{390}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la terraza, la sala, la planta, el ascensor and la piscina, and name five parts of a building.}

Complete ES-C390-piscina: name five parts of a building, and say one thing about each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la terraza]{la terraza — earth, flattened out and stood on}

\label{lesson:ES-C390-terraza}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I know how to read}. (\emph{Sé leer}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la tierra — the root underneath this one.
  \item el café — where you will hear the word most often.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{te-RRA-za}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{rr} is rolled, held a moment longer than a single tap. The \emph{z} is a soft \emph{s} across the Americas and a \emph{th} across much of Spain. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la terraza} — an open flat outdoor level: a roof terrace, a balcony floor, and above all the tables a café sets out on the pavement.

Latin \textbf{terra} was earth. From it came a Vulgar Latin \textbf{terrācea}, \textquotedblleft{}earthen\textquotedblright{} — a thing made of packed dirt. That much is certain, and the family is wide: English has \textbf{terrain}, \textbf{terrestrial}, \textbf{terra cotta}.

English \textbf{terrace} is not a relative but the same word, arriving through French. The twelfth-century Old French gloss is worth quoting because it is the evidence rather than a guess: \emph{a platform raised on a mound of earth faced with turf}. Not tiles. Not pottery. A flat place you built by heaping up soil and laying grass over the front of it, so you could stand above the ground.

Now the part that has to be said carefully, because the references disagree with each other and none of them is a fool.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item The Academy's dictionary keeps it at home, deriving \emph{terraza} from \emph{terrazo} inside Spanish.
  \item Wiktionary calls it \textquotedblleft{}more likely borrowed\textquotedblright{} from French \textbf{terrasse}, which took it from Old Occitan \textbf{terrassa}.
  \item And Corominas, going through everything that grew out of \emph{tierra}, does not list \emph{terraza} among them at all.
\end{itemize}

So: \emph{terra} is certain, and the road from \emph{terra} to \emph{terraza} is not. When three careful sources give three answers, the answer is that nobody knows yet.

One thing to refuse. English calls a row of joined houses a \emph{terrace}, and that sense is English-only, dated to 1769. A Spanish \emph{terraza} is never a house.

\begin{quote}
\emph{un café con terraza} — a café with tables outside.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the flat open space outside: \emph{la terraza}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la terraza}
  \item \emph{un café con terraza}
  \item \emph{estamos en la terraza}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{terrācea} mean? (Earthen — made of packed earth.) Does \emph{terraza} name a terraced house? (No. That row-of-houses sense is English only; a \emph{terraza} is an open flat level, usually a café's outdoor tables.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la sala]{la sala — the one Germanic room in a Latin house}

\label{lesson:ES-C390-sala}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the terrace}, then \emph{a café with tables outside}. (\emph{La terraza}; \emph{un café con terraza}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la casa — what this is a room of.
  \item la habitación — the neighbouring word.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SA-la}, two beats with the weight on the first. Both \emph{a}s are the same open sound, neither of them swallowed. The \emph{s} stays clear and hissed; the \emph{l} is bright, made with the tongue tip forward. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la sala} — the main room of a house, the living room; also a large room put to public use.

Nearly everything in a Spanish house came from Latin. This did not.

Behind \emph{sala} is Proto-Germanic \textbf{salaz}, and what it named was a \emph{one-room building}. The house was the room and the room was the house. Its relatives sit across the old Germanic languages: Old High German \textbf{sal}, Old English \textbf{sele}, Old Norse \textbf{salr}, all on a very old root meaning a dwelling.

English then borrowed it back out of French, twice over. \textbf{Salon} came in during the 1690s; \textbf{saloon} followed. English's own inherited form of the word is \textbf{sele}, which survives only in old poetry.

One pairing to keep out, because it looks irresistible and is wrong: English \textbf{hall} is \emph{not} this word. It comes from a separate Germanic form, \emph{hallō}. Two Germanic words for large rooms, two different ancestries.

Now the honest part. Germanic words reached Spanish by more than one road — Gothic speakers in the peninsula, and Frankish words passing down through Catalan and southern France — and for \emph{sala} Corominas refuses to pick. He calls it \textbf{inseguro} whether it arrived through Catalan and Gallo-Romance or straight from Gothic, and settles on there having been \textbf{varios focos de difusión}, several separate points from which it spread. The one story he throws out flatly, as \textbf{inadmisible}, is that it came from France alone.

One firm date: \emph{sala} is on record as a proper name in a Leonese document of \textbf{1102}.

Two lookalikes that are not family: \emph{sal}, salt, is Latin \textbf{sāl}; \emph{salir} is Latin \textbf{salīre}, to jump. Neither touches a room.

\begin{quote}
\emph{una sala grande} — a big living room.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the room a house is lived in: \emph{la sala}. And you know one Spanish noun that came in from the north instead of from Rome.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la sala}
  \item \emph{una sala grande}
  \item \emph{la sala y la terraza}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \emph{sala} a Latin word? (No — Germanic, from \emph{salaz}, a one-room building.) Did it come to Spanish through France? (Corominas says that story alone is inadmissible; the routes were several, and which one carried it is uncertain.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la planta]{la planta — a book word with a mouth-worn twin}

\label{lesson:ES-C390-planta}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the terrace}, then \emph{the living room}. (\emph{La terraza}; \emph{la sala}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el piso — the everyday word alongside this one.
  \item el pie — where the Latin word starts.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PLAN-ta}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{l} is bright, made with the tongue tip forward, and the \emph{pl} stays a crisp pair with nothing slipped between them. The \emph{t} is dental — tongue against the back of the top teeth, not up on the ridge. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la planta} — a floor of a building, a storey.

Latin \textbf{planta} carried two senses at once: the \textbf{sole of the foot}, and a \textbf{cutting}, a shoot pressed down into soil. English kept them both and kept them apart. \emph{Plantar}, as in plantar fasciitis, is the sole. \emph{Plant} and \emph{plantation} are the cutting. Whether Latin had one word doing two jobs or two words that fell together, the references disagree — Corominas suspects \textbf{dos vocablos distintos}; Wiktionary concludes they are one and the same.

Here is the best thing in the word, and it is visible in the first two letters.

Look at what happened to Latin \emph{pl-} in words Spanish inherited by mouth, worn down by ordinary speakers over centuries:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{plēnum} $\to$ \textbf{lleno}
  \item \emph{plūvia} $\to$ \textbf{lluvia}
  \item \emph{plicāre} $\to$ \textbf{llegar}
\end{itemize}

Every one of them came out with \emph{ll-}. So \emph{planta}, which still has its \emph{pl-} intact, did not come down that road. Corominas states the inference outright: \textbf{el tratamiento de \emph{pl-} indica que ha de ser cultismo} — the treatment of the \emph{pl-} shows it has to be a word taken from writing.

The mouth-worn twin is not hypothetical: \textbf{llanta}, which in the \emph{Partidas} meant a vegetable. One Latin word, two routes, two shapes — the spoken one bent, the written one preserved.

Careful with that twin: \emph{llanta} is really two words — the cabbage-plant one from \emph{planta}, and a wheel rim from elsewhere. Corominas separates them.

One question stays open, and it is the sense used here. How \emph{planta} came to name a \textbf{storey} is not settled: Corominas declines to decide — \textbf{no está bastante estudiado el problema} — leaving Italian and a home-grown development both open.

\begin{quote}
\emph{la primera planta} — the first floor.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can say which floor of a building you mean: \emph{la planta}. And you can read a surviving \emph{pl-} as a fingerprint of a word that came in through writing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la planta}
  \item \emph{la primera planta}
  \item \emph{la sala está en la primera planta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What shape did \emph{plēnum}, \emph{plūvia} and \emph{plicāre} come out in? (\emph{Lleno}, \emph{lluvia}, \emph{llegar} — the \emph{pl-} arrived as \emph{ll-}.) So what does the surviving \emph{pl-} of \emph{planta} tell you? (That it was not worn down by speech; it was lifted out of written Latin.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el ascensor]{el ascensor — an old word waiting for its machine}

\label{lesson:ES-C390-ascensor}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the living room}, then \emph{the first floor}. (\emph{La sala}; \emph{la primera planta}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item subir — what it does.
  \item la escalera — what people used before it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{as-cen-SOR}, three beats with the weight on the last. The \emph{c} before \emph{e} is soft, so the middle beat begins with an \emph{s} sound and the written \emph{sc} comes out as one clean hiss. The final \emph{r} is a single tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el ascensor} — the elevator.

It takes apart cleanly. Latin \textbf{ascēnsor} is an agent noun — a \emph{-tor} word, the one who does the thing — built on \textbf{ascendere}. And \emph{ascendere} is \textbf{ad-}, \textquotedblleft{}to, up to,\textquotedblright{} plus \textbf{scandere}, \textquotedblleft{}to climb.\textquotedblright{} So the whole word says: \emph{the one who ascends}. Nothing about cables, cars or shafts is in there.

The Romans had the word for eighteen centuries before anyone had the machine, and it is worth seeing what they used it for. In the Vulgate, at Exodus 15, the \textbf{ascensor} is a \textbf{horseman} — the rider, the one gone up onto the horse. That is who an ascender was.

So the form and the meaning came by different roads, and the meaning has a date. French \textbf{ascenseur} existed in the early sixteenth century and meant a rider too. The sense we want — \emph{an apparatus that serves to go up} — is recorded by the CNRTL for the first time in \textbf{1867}. Spanish \emph{ascensor} is therefore ancient in shape and modern in what it points at: a Latin word handed a nineteenth-century job.

The English family is large and regular. From \emph{ascendere}: \textbf{ascend}, \textbf{ascent}, \textbf{ascension}. From the \emph{scandere} underneath it: \textbf{descend}, \textbf{transcend}, and \textbf{scansion} — climbing along the beats of a line of verse.

One that is not family, however much it looks it: \textbf{scandal}. That comes from Greek \emph{skandalon} and has no share in this.

\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Dónde está el ascensor?} — Where is the elevator?
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can ask for the elevator: \emph{el ascensor}. And you can tell an old form from a young meaning wearing it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el ascensor}
  \item \emph{¿dónde está el ascensor?}
  \item \emph{subo a la primera planta en el ascensor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Who was an \emph{ascēnsor} in the Vulgate? (A horseman — the one gone up onto the horse.) When does the machine sense first appear? (In French, in 1867.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la piscina]{la piscina — one Latin fish, two Spanish roads}

\label{lesson:ES-C390-piscina}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the first floor}, then \emph{where is the elevator?}. (\emph{La primera planta}; \emph{¿dónde está el ascensor?})
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el agua — what fills it.
  \item el pescado — the fish you eat, built on the same \emph{piscis}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pis-CI-na}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is soft, so that beat is \emph{see} across the Americas and \emph{thee} across much of Spain. Both \emph{i}s are tight and bright, never sliding toward an \emph{uh}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la piscina} — a swimming pool.

Latin \textbf{piscīna} is \textbf{piscis}, a fish, with the ending \textbf{-īna} on it.

The cleanest thing here is a pair. That same Latin root reached Spanish twice, by two roads, and the two arrivals look nothing alike:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pez} — inherited, carried down by mouth, worn short;
  \item \textbf{piscina} — taken out of writing, its shape kept whole.
\end{itemize}

One root, two routes. (\emph{Piscīna} has a worn-down double of its own, \textbf{pecina}.)

Now a warning about the gloss, because the tempting move is wrong. \emph{Piscina} does not mean \textquotedblleft{}fishpond\textquotedblright{} in Spanish, and Spanish did not stretch it from fish to swimmers. That stretch had already happened in Rome. Lewis and Short mark the bathing sense as a post-Augustan transfer, and it turns up in Pliny, Seneca and Martial. Spanish borrowed the word with that meaning already attached.

English holds the root twice: \textbf{fish} is the inherited cousin of \emph{piscis}, the Latin \emph{p} answering a Germanic \emph{f}. Borrowed straight from Latin: \textbf{Pisces}, \textbf{piscine}, \textbf{piscatorial}.

Before you travel: Mexico often says \textbf{alberca}, the Río de la Plata \textbf{pileta} — not variants but separate words, \emph{alberca} from Arabic \emph{al-birka}, \emph{pileta} Romance.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name five parts of a building: \emph{la terraza}, \emph{la sala}, \emph{la planta}, \emph{el ascensor}, \emph{la piscina}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la piscina}
  \item \emph{la piscina y el ascensor}
\end{itemize}

Now all five together. Name each part of the building, then say one thing about it.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la terraza — la terraza es pequeña}
  \item \emph{la sala — la sala es grande}
  \item \emph{la planta — vivo en la primera planta}
  \item \emph{el ascensor — el ascensor sube}
  \item \emph{la piscina — la piscina está abajo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \emph{pez} and \emph{piscina} came down by mouth? (\emph{Pez}.) Did Spanish turn a fishpond into a swimming pool? (No — the Romans had already done it; the swimming sense came with the word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
